newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi backs Burma bid for ASEAN, seeks closer ties.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi backs Burma bid for ASEAN, seeks closer ties.

text.p: Vietnam on Thursday reiterated its support for Burma's early membership in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and called for closer ties with Rangoon.
The official Vietnam News Agency said that was the message that Foreign Minister Nguyen Manh Cam had for his Burmese counterpart, Ohn Gyaw, who arrived in Hanoi on Wednesday.

"Warmly welcoming him...Cam expressed his hope for further development of the Vietnam-Myanmar (Burma) cooperation and Vietnam's support for early accession of Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia to ASEAN," it said.

Last month's informal ASEAN summit in Indonesia ended with a declaration that the seven-member regional grouping would simultaneously admit Burma, Laos and Cambodia as full members. But it gave no date for when that might happen.

The announcement followed reservations voiced by members Philippines, Thailand and Singapore on early Burmese membership following renewed crackdowns on the opposition party of Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.

Ohn Gyaw, who will attend the second session of a bilateral joint committee on Friday, said he hoped his visit would help boost cooperation in the interest of each country and for the sake of regional stability and development.
He thanked Hanoi for supporting Burma's aim to join ASEAN this year.
A Hanoi official, who declined to be named, said Cam and Ohn Gyaw discussed economic cooperation in agriculture, forestry and the gemstone industry.

He said they also discussed coordination on controlling trade in narcotics. Vietnam is a market and transit route for narcotics from the notorious opium-growing Golden Triangle, the area where Laos, Thailand and Burma meet.

European countries and the United States have proposed sanctions against Burma, and some diplomats say Burma's admission as a full member to ASEAN would be tantamount to approval of its military government's policies.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and, since 1995, Vietnam.
